newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Economists say AFTA will prove costly to Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Economists say AFTA will prove costly to Cambodia.

text.p: Cambodia's entry into the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) could cripple the nation's economy unless it counters an over-reliance on customs revenues, senior finance officials said on Tuesday.

Finance Minister Keat Chhon and Aun Porn Moniroth, the ministry's senior economic official, said reducing Cambodia's customs duties -- about 72 percent of total tax revenues -- required strong political will and ambitious tax reform.

Cambodia is likely to join the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) by the middle of this year and then will soon be expected to join AFTA and take steps to implement its Agreement on Common Effective Preferential Tariff (CEPT).
"We will have to make progess under pressure," said Aun Porn Moniroth.

The two economists, who said they were speaking in their private capacities rather than on behalf of the government, also warned that AFTA's tariff reductions may worsen Cambodia's negative balance of payments and lack of competitiveness.
They spoke at a press conference marking the release of an AFTA discussion paper they co-authored on behalf of a Phnom Penh think tank, the Cambodian Institute for Cooperation and Peace.

Joining AFTA does bring long-term opportunities, including increased access to international markets and job creation, but of immediate concern is the costly short-term effects of lowering tariffs, Aun Porn Moniroth said.

"Cambodia should not rush into determining its time frame (for tariff reductions) because we are not sure yet about the impact on the budget," he said, noting that Cambodia was expected to take about 10 years to fall in line with CEPT.

ASEAN established AFTA in January 1992 to attract investment, ensure the competitiveness of member nations in international markets and liberalise trade within the grouping by reducing custom tariffs and eliminating non-tariff barriers.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Cambodia, Laos and Burma have observer status in the organisation.
